Params.Value: A guest locker beneath the cloth. Claim it while your guest-right holds; afterward the same chest remains available when the oath expires.
Two utility volumes are lent for Ink. Study grants their ordinary permanent knowledge. Return one book for the stated partial Ink refund, or buy out your exact loan in drams.
An abandoned screen still interrupts the view. Strip it for two lengths of knotflax cord and the cover is gone.
A short dry crossing is watched from this post. Four drams buy one local passage. The longer dry boardwalks and the wet crossing remain open.
This watcher guards only the marked cutbank. Pay before entering, take the longer boards, or wade. A passage does not excuse a personal attack.
An ordinary gate keeps the grazer from the outside forage row. Open it and the animal can follow the real path out.
Old counter stock remains behind a keyed lock. A key, a nearby locksmith, or breaking the box will expose the same finite goods.
A thin conjured acid film. Anything crossing it is coated in acid. It fades after four turns and cannot be gathered.

This marlback carries a spark root in a dry pouch beneath blue-stained shale plates. It soaks a clear target, then sends lightning along the same line. Break its sight, dry off, or close while its spells recover. It keeps a little distance, steps around blocked shots, and will spend time recovering its own dropped cudgel.
Blue-stained shale plates are folded over the still claws of a stormbinder. The dry pouch and any unspent supplies fell with their owner.
A shaped length of salvaged timber. Strength modifier cap 1; no hit or penetration bonus.
A plain knotflax lashing. Fits a forged weapon; no hit or penetration bonus.
Sandstone patiently cut from tepuibone into a small striking head. Cudgel family; 1d3 damage and -1 penetration. No reach bonus.
Bracing carries a strong wielder's force at the cost of precision. Strength modifier cap 5; -1 hit.
A close balanced lashing. +2 hit, -1 penetration; no extra armor or reach.

Wear on your head instead of a helmet. Filters 50 points of respiratory intake and reduces typed gas damage by 10%. It is not gas immunity, armor, or a cure for existing poison. Its leather fastening seams can be repaired with one leather binding when damaged.

A sealed work apron. Body AV 1, DV -1, speed -5; +50 acid resistance while worn. Other damage is unchanged, and one-point acid hits still hurt. Its leather fastening seams can be repaired with one leather binding when damaged.

A heavy-folded coldward cloak. Back AV 0, DV -1; +50 cold resistance while worn. Replaces your other back garment; no immunity. Its leather fastening seams can be repaired with one leather binding when damaged.
Apply one bandage to stop ordinary bleeding. No healing, poison cure or lasting protection. Application spends the bandage even when no bleeding is present.
You bind the wound with knotflax.
Two sprigs reduced to one portable measure. Brew into one 2d4 healing draught instead of two separate 1d4 draughts.
Two sprigs reduced to one measure at an alchemy still. Vitality is concentrated: vital 2. Brew it for 2d4 healing.
Processed grove-red: toxic character removed, original vital potency reduced to 2. Brew for 2d4 healing.
The bitter toxic fraction has been discarded at a still. Vital 2; no toxic property. This process does not mend the grove.

A split-legged dressing bench with a cloth clamp and a bitter-leaf press. Sella needs two sound timber lengths to brace it. The abandoned cutting works lie two stretches east, beyond the cutbank crossing. Once repaired, the keeper wraps one sumpsieve pad and one knotflax cord into a field dressing for two drams. Dressings treat existing ordinary poison and bleeding; they do not protect against marsh gas.

Four sound timber lengths remain in this abandoned drying frame. Harvest them once. Two will brace the dressing bench at the shelter two stretches west; sound timber also serves other wooden repairs and mechanical trap jamming.

An iron-banded locker survives above the old wet line. Its remaining equipment and cord can be taken; nobody replenishes these abandoned stores. Leather boots and a buckler offer their usual armor, not immunity to mire or marsh gas.
Cutters have left a route notice above the wet line. The shelter, crossing and abandoned works form a short southern circuit below Sumphold.

Sumpsieve folded into a tight knotflax wrap. Apply it to remove existing ordinary poison and bleeding together. A dressing is used only when one of those conditions is present. It does not restore health, cure gas poisoning or fungal infection, or protect against future exposure.
A shallow bed of leftover cooking coals. Its remaining heat will fade.
Stoppered squid-dark ink. The quartermasters take payment in it; the scribes never seem to run out.
A short blade with a close-fitting grip. The point has been kept sharp.
A short-faced bank burrower with a broad back of overlapping shale plates. Its grasping foreclaws rake loose earth into low walls around the burrow mouth.
Overlapping shale plates lie slack above short limbs and broad digging claws. Mud still fills the seams of the bank burrower’s back.
A low stone shelf under a lean-to, set with smooth stones, candle stubs and a bowl with a few coins in it. Whose shrine it is depends on who you ask. Everyone agrees it is a good place to stop.
Discarded cutting tools sit between this marlback’s shale back plates. It works the river wrack with a blunt snout and quick grasping claws, retreating toward its burrow when pressed.

Pale straps cross this marlback's shale plates. A little open cradle sits within reach of its grasping claws, padded with old cloth; its cutting tools are kept farther back. The harness has been patched far more carefully than its owner's scars.

This short-faced marlback braces a salvaged pole across the passage. Pale shale plates overlap its broad back; hooked digging claws grip the wet bank beneath it. If disarmed, it spends separate actions retrieving and re-equipping its own weapon; taking that weapon away denies the recovery.
A toxic chill spreads through the body.
Heat blooms outward in a violent flash.

Cutters around Sumphold pack peat with this broad iron-faced head. Forged as a cudgel, its bludgeoning blows can stun and it supports learned cudgel skills. It trades damage and armor penetration for control: head damage 1d4, penetration -1. Add a haft and binding in the Crafting tab. The abandoned works east of the cutbank kept these with their pump screens.

A heavy hooked edge from Cinderhold extraction crews, sold by the workshop smith. Assemble it with a haft and binding to use learned axe skills. The hook bites hard but pulls a swing wide: head damage 1d8, hit -2. A steadier haft or binding can offset that cost; the crafting preview shows the final weapon.

Last Counter keeps these slender frontier blades in its supply-post chest. A brass counterweight steadies the point; the thin edge struggles against armor. Head damage 1d6, hit +1, penetration -1. A haft and binding make a long blade for learned stances and Lunge. The weapon does not teach those skills.

Cinderhold kiln workers stitch mineral felt beneath overlapping red patches. Worn on the body, it gives 50 heat resistance but only 1 armor and slows you by 5. It sacrifices physical protection for fire and steam work; it does not protect against poison gas, acid, cold or electricity. The workshop smith sells the apron beside the cinderhook heads.

A handgrip and insulated backing have been fitted to the copper mesh once used to earth peatworks pumps. It gives 50 electrical resistance while held, occupying a hand that could carry a shield or weapon. The open mesh gives no armor or dodge bonus and does not protect against mire acid or poison. Spare screens remain in the abandoned works locker east of the cutbank.
Warm to the touch; crumbles with a spark. (heat, volatile)
Slow, greasy, eager to burn. (combustible, viscous)
A slow warmth lingers on the tongue. (heat, sweet)
Rimed fronds that ache the fingertips. (cold)
Cracks with a deep, patient chill; sets like mortar. (cold, binding)
Stings the nose; hums faintly against the jar. (corrosive, conductive)
Hairs rise near its severed end. (conductive)
Harvested from something that bit first. (toxic)
Clinging tar with a sour reek. (toxic, viscous)
Beats faintly. Tastes of nothing much. (vital, sweet)
Hard as a knuckle; sets like mortar. (binding)
Do not shake. Do not warm. (volatile, combustible)
A pale seed, faintly sweet-smelling, the size of a fingernail. Plant it in soft ground.
A warm golden grain that never quite cools. Plant it in soft ground.
Crisp and orange and honest about it. Grown, not made.
Cool mist rises from the pages. You learn Conjure Rain.
The rite of rain is already yours.
A damp-smelling tome whose ink never quite dries. Its pages describe how to call small, polite rainclouds down onto growing things.
A sheaf of grain that glows faintly warm, even at night.
Caustic green liquid hisses against your skin.
Static crackles across your skin and hair stands on end.
An ice-cold draught freezes you from the inside.
Cool water, all the way down.
Sharp pain blooms — your wounds reopen.
Bitter ash coats your tongue — your skin hardens against future fire.
The bitter tonic neutralizes the poison.
A warm light floods through you, purging all afflictions.
Panels of thick leather are joined where the body needs to bend. The fastening straps show repeated use.
Small metal rings overlap in a flexible mesh. Their weight gathers wherever the garment folds.
Interwoven stems have thickened into a wall. More growth knots around the older strands.
A woody trunk rises from a spread of roots. Branches fill the space above it.
A seat and back are joined above a set of legs. The places hands rest are worn smooth.
Straw fills the sleeping place. The top has been pressed flat and gathered up again.
A long, straight blade balanced above a plain crossguard.
A broad axe head sits on a reinforced haft. The cutting edge curves away from the socket.
A large blade with room for both hands on the hilt. Its reach begins well beyond the grip.
A compact sword with a straight edge and enough grip to keep the hand behind the guard.
A heavy head on a short haft. Its raised faces concentrate the weight of a blow.
A narrow point extends from a long shaft. The join is bound close beneath the head.
A short haft carries a wedge-shaped head. The back of the blade is thick enough to take a knock.
A broad sword with a long grip and a guard that spreads well clear of the blade.
A stout club, heavier at the striking end and smoothed where a hand holds it.
A small shield with a raised centre and a grip behind it.
A worked iron shell with an opening for the face. The rim has been turned away from the skin.
Supple leather boots with thicker soles and reinforced seams around the toes.
Close-fitting gloves with extra leather across the palms.
A fitted leather cap, stitched in curved panels to follow the head.
Iron strengthens the soles of these boots. Scuffs mark the places that meet the ground first.
Fine stitching follows the edges of this cloak. The repeated pattern continues around the fastening.
A compact iron shield. Its turned rim leaves a shallow bowl behind the face.
Shaped plates overlap at the joints, with straps holding each section against the body.
A broad piece of cloth with a fastening at the neck. Its hem carries the wear of travel.
The tonic sends a quicksilver rush through the body.

Salted strips that travel well, until their smell finds company. Drop or throw it onto ground a hunting furrowstalker can see, then stay out of sight. It may stop to eat once during that hunt. Approaching it can still provoke an attack; throwing meat at it is an attack.
Forearms like bridge cables. The ring of the forge follows them around.
Measures you with a glance and starts thinking in buckles and plates.
Smells of forty herbs at once. Knows which twelve could kill you.
Ink-stained fingers, a shelf of humming grimoires, and prices to match.
Sacks, jars, bundles, barrels. If it keeps on a shelf, they stock it.
An old soul grown half into the moss. Keeps a kettle on for travelers.
Sun-cured and patient. They say the dunes talk to those who stop hurrying.
Fingers stained green and black. Knows every leaf that kills and every leaf that saves.
Tends a lamp older than the ruins around it. Remembers what the stones forgot.
A dense striking head is fixed across a long handle. The face is narrower than the mass behind it.

A single page, wax-sealed, the Concord's counting-house hand. The clause is short: the tendrils at the grove edges are to be pruned to the surveyed line by the posted date. A margin note, initialed: post where the grove can read it.
Layers of dark shale broaden this marlback’s back above a patched digging harness. It keeps a long cutting tool ready beside the low wall of its burrow.
Heavy shale plates crowd the shoulders of this blunt-faced marlback. It carries a wedge-cleaver made for splitting roots and swings its weight forward with each stubborn step.
A salvaged wedge-blade lashed to a short haft. Shale grit fills its binding; the broad edge is worn from splitting roots and breaking packed banks.
Soft silver-veined leaves that close when it rains. The herbalists strip them gently; the rotlings just eat the whole plant.
Low branches and leaves form a close tangle near the ground.
Stones mark a place for a fire. Ash has collected between them.
Jointed stems stand close together, with narrow leaves folded along their sides.
compass stone pointing north toward the Ruins of Sparkwright
compass stone pointing east toward the Saltglass Dunes
compass stone pointing south toward the Verdant Rotbog
compass stone pointing west toward the Frostfang Grotto

Fresh flesh; useful food, or a costly distraction. Drop or throw it onto ground a hunting furrowstalker can see, then stay out of sight. It may stop to eat once during that hunt. Approaching it can still provoke an attack; throwing meat at it is an attack.
Hands and hauled ropes have polished the rim. The water lies below.
A counter gives someone a place to set out goods. Trading belongs to whoever tends it.
A hinged lid closes over a deep storage box. The frame is reinforced at the corners.
A salt-sealed drawer beside the Indexer's desk, its lead-line pressed into the lid: "Keeping is not the same as showing." Curation's files open for the words, or not at all.
A long iron key, its bow worn smooth by one hand over many years. A Curation file tag still hangs from it: filed with the keeper of Stillleaf.

A bound register in pale covers, the name Stillleaf pressed into its spine. It lists what this archive held — shelf, hand and year for every entry — and nothing of what the entries said. A slate is tied to the cover in the keeper's hand: 'Whoever carries this out: I sealed this place so that it would stay sealed. Not because what is here is dangerous. Because it was given to me to keep, and keeping is not the same as showing. If you take it, choose who holds it after you as carefully as I chose no one.'
Low mounds in rows, each marked with a stone or a stick. Someone keeps this ground; the newest earth is still dark.
You study the faded ink carefully. The rite of water purification takes shape in your mind.
You study the diagrams of force and fracture. The mending rite settles into your hands.
You trace the warding sigils with your eyes. The kindle rite sparks to life in your memory.
Flame-script blazes across the page. The kindle rite burns itself into your mind.
You already know the kindle rite.
Water-words ripple across the vellum. The quench rite flows into your memory.
You already know the quench rite.
The pages ignite as you read, yet do not burn. The conflagration rite sears itself into your will.
You already know the conflagration rite.
Crystalline glyphs bite your fingertips. The ice lance rite chills into your mind.
You already know the ice lance rite.
Corrosive ink hisses as you read. The acid spray rite eats its way into your mind.
You already know the acid spray rite.
Static crackles across the vellum. The arc bolt rite sparks into your memory.
You already know the arc bolt rite.
Frost lances spiral from the margins. The rime nova rite buries itself in your will.
You already know the rime nova rite.
Thunder rolls from the open pages. The thunderclap rite booms itself into your will.
You already know the thunderclap rite.
A vein of embers traces the page. The ember vein rite burns itself into your will.
You already know the ember vein rite.
Warm script flickers in the margins. You learn kindle flame.
The page exhales a dry wind. You learn drying breeze.
Steady embers glow between the lines. You learn hearthwarm.
Condensation beads across the page. You learn conjure water.
A biting draft slips from the pages. You learn chill draft.
The ink brightens to a cleansing sheen. You learn ward gleam.
The whetstone angles, the draw-stroke counts -- the honing pattern settles into your hands.
Overlap the plates like river-scale, the notes say. You see how it carries the blow.
The tailoring lines are drawn for someone who plans to be missed. You take the pattern.
A seam of light-hoarding quartz. It hums faintly when you stand close.
Crystallized white salt threaded through the limestone. The dead are said to hate it.
Dark ore that rings like a struck bell when chipped. The Rot Choir prizes it.
Wild berries cluster among the leaves. The fruit can be gathered.
Wax cells crowd the inside. Some hold honey.
A weathered post with arms pointing off toward places. Fresh cuts cross the old grain.
Boards enclose a cargo space. Its corners bear the marks of lifting and stacking.
Coarse cloth is gathered at the mouth. The folds conceal whatever has been packed inside.
A close weave rises to a stiff rim, making a light container for things that need carrying.
The centre of the wood is hollow. The opening leaves room to store small things inside.
A shelf lying on its face. Whatever books it held have swollen into one grey block of pulp, but people still tuck things behind the boards.
Thunder pools in the gutter of the page. The storm anvil is yours to bring down.
You already know the storm anvil.
The bolt hangs in the margin, refusing to fall. You learn to hold it there.
You already know the hanging bolt.
The page fogs and clears. Water and fire, held together just long enough.
Condensation beads, then hisses away. What soaks you can also shield you.
You already know the scalding veil.
The page holds a single instruction: put the charge down, and let it find its own way.
Frost creeps from the spine as you read. What is frozen is not armoured — it is brittle.
The page is cold and very quiet. You learn how to make a heart forget to hurry.
Green rot flowers across the margin and eats the gilding. The bloom takes root in your hands.
A coin is pressed into the page, worn smooth on both faces. Whatever is owed, it pays.
One word, written far too many times. Reading it once is enough to leave things smaller.
Two columns, in two different inks. You learn which side of the ledger to stand on.
Runs overhead and underfoot. Charge takes it and keeps going.
Salt water. Conducts better than fresh and freezes later.
Corroded, but iron still carries a charge.
Slow, thick and very willing to burn.
Catches from almost nothing and burns out fast.
Still hot. Water poured on it comes back up as steam.
Wet AND flammable — the one tile that answers to either school.
Breathes cold. Standing water near it will not stay liquid.
Frozen water still carries a charge — and it is brittle.
Wet and hot at once. Carries charge like the water it came from.
Oak, banded, and full of something. It will not go in a pack, but it will go across a floor.
A wheel of grey stone with a square hole through the middle. Off its spindle it is just a very heavy circle.
Not hard to move because it is heavy. Hard to move because there is nowhere to hold it.
A lidded box cut from one block. Whoever put it here did not expect it to leave.
A roof timber, down and lying where it landed. One end is charred.
Kept, and heavy with it. The salt has taken up residence in every part that used to be soft.
A wall of hawthorn and bramble, laid and woven by somebody's grandparents. It marks a boundary that no longer has a court to argue it.
Cut emberwheat stubble in an old field strip. The grain has already been gathered.
A few ripe emberwheat heads stand above the cut rows. Gather this gleaning by hand; the stubble will remain.
Packed earth over old stone, rutted by cartwheels. It goes somewhere, which is more than most things here do.
Pale bells on thin stems, growing where nobody sowed them. They are said to keep. Nobody in the Spread can tell you what they keep away.
Petals someone hummed up for the season, a carved token half-buried underneath for whichever river-god still gets the offerings here. It won't last.
A worn stone by the water, carved tokens left in its lap for whichever river-god still gets the offerings here. The Tree is a children's story in a place like this.
The pan cracked into plates as it dried. The ridges are sharp enough to read by.
Soft sand stacked steeper than it looks. Easier to go around than over.
Picked clean and dried white. Whatever it was, it was walking the road.
A big banded lizard basking flat on the crust, all display and speed. It holds its ground like it owns the noon.
A grey briar that grows where nothing should, its leaves rimed with the pan's own salt. Caravans strip it as they pass.
Woven goat-hair, dense enough to keep the noon out. The wall of a house that moves.
A dark cloth on a straight pole, hung where it can be seen from a long way off. What it offers holds for three days. Anyone following you knows what it means.
Weathered, unhurried, watching the road the way a well-keeper watches the water level.
A planed board in the Concord's neat hand: WE CANNOT GUARANTEE DELIVERY BEYOND THIS POINT. Underneath, older and fainter, the same words twice more.

A planed board in the Concord's neat hand: SURVEYED LINE AS POSTED. PRUNING BY THE DATE BELOW. The date has been scraped off and rewritten in a fresher ink, and the line beneath it is drawn straighter than the ground it describes.
White to the elbows. The scales beside the ledger are cleaner than anything else in the camp.
Tea-dark and still. It holds what it takes; the bog country is patient that way.
Planks laid on posts over the soft ground, worn smooth down the middle. Some of them answer your weight.
Grey wood standing in the water it drowned in. It kept its shape better than its neighbors.
Cut peat, the tool marks still clean. The bank face is layered like a book nobody meant to write.
A body the peat kept. Tanned dark as the water that took it; the knot in its cloak-cord is still a knot. It was not buried. It fell, and the bog wrote it down.

Older than the peat that holds it, and whole to the fingernails. A tin tag on waxed cord, Palimpsest work: 'Recension XI. Body-reading yields: leaf-light through high rooms; a name spoken to a tree, and answered. Reading incomplete.' The attribution is the expedition's. The body says nothing.
Fat, green, and unbothered until you are close enough to matter. The peat-cutters render them for lamp oil and know which pools they breed in, and guard that knowing like money.
Banded scarlet over black, and the bands are not decoration. Everything in the bog knows not to touch it; the lesson is the skin.
Mostly mouth. It sits where the dead trees stand in the water and it does not chase, because it has never needed to.
A bent stem strung with beads of something clearer than water. The beads do not fall. What it holds, it holds gently, and for exactly as long as it pleases; what it lets go walks away thinner.

Rendered fat in a stoppered gourd. Spread it onto nearby ground to leave slippery grease for eight turns. It can trip a pursuer or your own feet, and catches fire. Silver sand gives firm footing over the slick.
A hull upside-down on trestles, ribs bare, seams waiting for pitch. Sumphold builds shallow and wide, for water that is mostly patience.

Bound crossing-counts under a rain-hood, a century deep and mould-spotted: carts, heads, coin, initials. One entry is pressed harder than the rest of its year: short count -- forgiven -- my error. The rolls do not record a face.
A numbered stake, paint gone grey. The numbering starts somewhere out of sight and does not appear to be close to done.

A long table under canvas, scrubbed pale. Straps, padded blocks, a folio stand: everything arranged so a body may be read without being moved more than it must be. The attending junior's stool sits where the light is worst.
Ink to the second knuckle, and a table of attributions never out of reach. Reads everything twice; asserts almost nothing.
A Recension Searcher, ink to the wrist like any scribe, but her table holds old survey maps instead of an attribution list. She reads catalogue fragments the way other people read letters from home.
Gloves, always. A ledger of numbered things, each entry ending in the same word. Handles everything as if it were on loan, which, per the files, it is.
A Pale Curation Indexer. Gloves to the elbow, a ledger open at the day's page, every entry led by a sentence somebody said last. They will argue a transcription for a week and file the argument.
Boots to the thigh and a blade like a long spade worn to a shine. Smells of smoke that never quite goes out.

Wrapped, waxed, and corded to Curation intake standard; the sorter's stamp is in the seal. The label, in a careful hand: one entry. Status: continuing. It is heavier than it looks, and it looks heavy.
The intake window of Marrowstye is a person at a table, and the person is this one. Stamps in a row, wax in a warmer, and a ledger whose every entry ends the same way.
A column of pale growth, waist-thick and faintly warm, veined violet under the skin. The light in the veins moves slowly, always in the same direction. It holds up nothing. It is not for holding up.
Clean water rising cold through white filaments, clearer than any well in the towns. The sign says it is for you. Nothing here has ever said otherwise.
Growth in shelves and closed fists, violet over ochre. It was not this size last season. It will not be this size next season.
Undercut rock at the rim, wet with spray from below. The green here grows thicker than the green anywhere else in the chunk, and leans in.
Not stone. The wall here was grown, in the way a bone is grown, and it is faintly warm where you rest a hand on it. Threads run through the violet in it, all of them going the same way.
Where every thread in the vault gathers and does not stop. The light off it is steady, and slow, and has the rhythm of something breathing very deeply somewhere a long way off.

A person, held. The substrate has taken everything below the shoulders and most of what was above them, and the face it has left is composed, and turned slightly toward you, and has been for a very long time.

Mature fungus in a low mound, breathing light the colour of new leaves. It is warm the way a body is warm. Everything in this room is arranged around it, and everyone in this room is watching you look at it.
A cell carved into the wall face, bedding folded at the back, a lamp-hook above. Someone sleeps here now and will be laid here later. It is not morbid. It is home.
Cut names, row on row, oldest at the floor. The village's history is not written down anywhere else; it is this wall.
Tended sundew, planted in a ring and kept that way. It catches what walks in and it is not sentimental about it.
A stoppered jar of lantern-beetles, hung at head height. They brighten when the room moves. Crush one and every Warden in the village will know inside a breath.
A tended field of small sundews across the entry, kept trimmed to ankle height. Stepping across is how the village is introduced to you.
RIANE. Patch-Tender. Widowed the year the green light came back. Tended forty years. Says the patch sang once, and no one believes her, and she does not care.
OSSU. Beetle-Master. Went upstairs young and came back old and never said. Good hands. The wall keeps him anyway.
MERRIN, called MOTH. Child. One winter. The light dimmed the night she went and the old people say it was courtesy.
— — — — — The stone here has been chiselled back to smooth. Nothing is cut into it, and the cutting that was there has been taken out to the depth of a thumbnail.

VASHTI. Tongue. Spoke for the village to three Factors, two Curators, and once, badly, to a god. First Plaque cut at twelve; died at ninety-one; the plaque she cut at twelve is behind this one, and it says, in a child's letters: I WILL SLEEP HERE WHEN I AM DONE. SAVE MY PLACE.
The letters here are worn beyond the alphabet. Whatever this row says, it has stopped saying it in any language now in use.
Broad through the shoulders, pale as the walls, and standing where the light from the patch falls across the entry. She has been watching you since the sundew.
Old, and holding a lamp low to the bottom rows. Her hands are chalked white to the wrist from re-cutting letters that were going soft.
A shelf of rock wide enough to stand on and not much wider. Water finds it, uses it, and goes on down.
A heavy pit viper the colour of wet stone, coiled where the litter is deepest. It does not rattle and it does not flee. Where these are thick on a slope, something underneath is awake.
A long olive colubrid draped along a branch, watching the ground with more attention than it spends on you. Villages that have one nearby say so the way other places mention a good well.

A thumbnail of a frog, pale-striped, sitting in the spray with a back full of young. It has no call. Where the water is good, they are everywhere; where the water has gone wrong, they are the first thing missing.
Its underside is a window. You can watch the heart work from here, which is a thing it cannot hide from you and does not seem to mind. The Bower-Folk pay for these alive and unbruised.
A tortoise the size of a footstool, going somewhere at its own rate. Some villages have kept one for six generations and treat it as the oldest thing that remembers them.
Pink-grey sandstone, worn smooth and faintly warm underfoot. Every tepui in the world is the Tree's anatomy turned to stone; this one is the stump itself, and you are standing on it.
A shoulder of pink stone standing out of the slope. The grain in it runs the same way the grain runs everywhere here, which is how you know the whole mountain is one object.
A ridge of pink-grey stone with the grain of wood in it, running the way every other ridge on this mountain runs. It is not like wood. It is wood, finished with being wood.
A dome of pink stone, smooth as a knuckle. It was a bough once, or the knot where a bough met the trunk. The scrub grows in its cracks and does not ask.

A bromeliad the size of a rain barrel, holding a barrel's worth of rain. The water is clear and cold and something small lives its entire life in there. Summit people drink from these and leave the small thing unbothered.
Falling water lands here and stands a while, cold and bright, before it finds the next shelf down. Things live in it that live nowhere drier.
An iron pin driven into the rock, and a hand's length of rope still knotted to it. The cut end is old and clean: somebody took the rest with them, or somebody took it from them.
Growth in shelves and closed fists, brighter than its neighbors, and warm. It is further along than the others. Standing near it feels like being considered.

A board of grown wood, the letters raised in living grain — grown out of it, not carved into it — and weathered smooth by hands. It reads: WALKER. YOU ARE ENTERING US. Walk anywhere. Everything is path. Drink at the seep. It is for you. Eat nothing red. The red is thinking. If you hear singing, it is old singing. It is not for you. You may listen anyway. The singers do not mind. The singers have not minded anything for a long time, and it is a kindness to be heard. Do not dig. If you are tired — truly tired, walker, the kind of tired that has stopped keeping count — lie down anywhere soft. Someone will cover you. If you are only a little tired, keep walking. We can tell the difference. We are patient about the difference. GO GENTLY. EVERYTHING HERE IS SOMEBODY.
No longer than a hand. The column beside it has grown around one arm, and stopped.

A tidy row of what is being taken back: cloth gone to lace, a boot, chitin, a shape further along than the rest. The rows are straight. Nothing made them straight; they grew that way. Everything here is somebody.
A fruit of astonishing health, grown from everyone the grove has ever loved. The red is thinking.
Low growth heavy with red, at the grove edge, where the sign can see it. The sign says eat nothing red. Nothing stops you picking it.

It was somebody's shape once, and the growth kept the shape because the shape still walked. Before lashing, it draws one tendril straight back. The lash follows that line for two paces; the body hangs loose while the tendril gathers again.
A wheezing pouch of spores. Keep it away from flame, and from your face, and honestly from you.
A hand-sized moth with broad translucent wings, each crossed by three soft bars of pale grove-light. It navigates by the columns; the glow is dust on its wings.
Leaves the color of wine going darker, beaded sticky at every edge. How dark the leaves are is how recently it has eaten. These are quite dark.
A spot in the row where the taking-back has further to go. Some of what comes up still has pockets. The grove does not mind; it was never after the pockets.
A small brown frog with a dark W folded across its back. It waits against a mossy trunk, throat lifted. One note, then another. The long space between them seems to belong to the mountain.
A lichen-coloured lizard flattened against the stone. Its green-brown flanks repeat the mottling of the dome so closely that the yellow eye seems to hang there alone. Tank leaves shiver close by.

An immense ash-pale eagle, dark beneath the wings. Its talons close slowly on nothing. People who know the slopes watch the ground when this shadow crosses them: what coils below and what circles above have begun keeping the same hours.

An indigo gecko with an amber throat and a long fine spine above each eye. It holds itself close to the litter, all sharp elbows and patient attention. Several small tracks meet beneath the stone beside it.

A broad-headed forest frog with a bony casque like a weathered wooden helm. A bead of water clings below its jaw. Underground, such a visitor is worth following: forest frogs do not arrive in sealed rooms.
Sixteen pale eggs share a hollow under the leaf litter. Blue-black brows watch from the surrounding cracks. A foot in that hollow would have many answers.
A pale seam holds its line through the pink-grey stone. The mountain remembers a grain older than rock. Even a loose chip seems unwilling to be lifted.
Sandstone cut from the Root. It weighs more than its size promises, pale grain closed tightly around the memory of wood. Name-holders work it patiently; the stone has never been in a hurry.

A chip of memory-marble worked loose from an archive wall: the Palimpsest's writing-surface, which holds what is written on it harder than the hand that wrote it. One of the three stones that hold their names hardest, and so one of the three that could hold the Root still.

Mute-stone, pale grey and warm nowhere. The death-watch is kept in chambers of it because it does not answer, and what does not answer cannot be unsaid. One of the three stones that hold their names hardest, and so one of the three that could hold the Root still.

A living thread of the Choir, cut and given, warm and faintly moving in the hand. Set against the sleeping Root it would take, the way water takes the way to the sea, and the Choir would reach what it has walked toward for a thousand years: nothing lost, no one left. It hums one syllable, patiently.
Fresh water runs through a low opening worn smooth in the stone. The current comes from farther away than this pool can explain. Stand here and follow it downward (>) or upward (<).

A human shape has grown into the stone: shins flat, knees bent, torso arched above the floor. Pale fungus rises from his chest. His open arms reach toward the eastern wall and stop short of it. Nothing has been built in that narrow distance. The pose holds no strain.
Pale stalks rise from the Rooted's torso and spread into a soft, warm bed. Every hearth in Olderdeep grew outward from this body. Those trusted by the Listening Tradition may lie here and sleep.
She rests one hand against the chamber wall as she listens. Her voice reaches you at the same volume as her breathing.
Stone dust whitens her knees. She deepens an old inscription one small cut at a time, pausing to speak toward the floor between cuts.
A shallow arc in the pink-grey grain, rounded as a crease in an old hand. It continues around an open circle.
Bare ground interrupts the circle. No root, moss or filament holds here. Five other patches face the same open space; none carries a name.
A seventh interval in the circle. Nothing occupies it. Looking across it, the near and far edges briefly cease to agree. The air is wrong at this one point.

The taproot's face, exposed where the stone gave way: sandstone-pale, warm to a hand laid flat, slower than breathing. It is the last living root of the Tree that held everything, and it is asleep. It dreams. What it dreams, no one who came down here has been able to say.
Pale stone closes in long courses. Grain turns through the blocks without reaching their edges.
Clouded bands repeat beneath the polished face. The joints are too fine to admit a fingertip.
Dull iron ribs bind the stone courses. Their rivets are set deep; no filament grows in the seams.
Iron lies flush within a pale stone frame. A small keyway interrupts the unbroken seam.
Close-fitted slabs run between the sealed shelves.
Tied bundles stand in shallow stone shelves. Faded clay seals close each binding.
Smooth ground. No stones break the surface.
A few pale shoots. Every tip reaches the same height.
A short stone at the edge of the blank ground. Its face carries no legible mark.
A plain wooden bench turned toward the empty ground.
Wide weathered boards braced into a low timber wall. Local carpenters replace one section at a time.
A broad writing desk, weighted against the crossing wind. This office keeps ordinary road and household records.
A portable timber counter with storage beneath its broad trading surface.
Exchange and stores; the records office; the caravan rest. Three stout arms point into the public courts of Gantry.
A Pale Curation clerk with wind-flattened sleeves and ordinary ink on both hands. Their work concerns the living: road accounts, tenancy and the careful spelling of names.
Clouded gray marble, fitted around a public reading room. Ordinary joints admit ordinary tools; this is a working archive, not a sealed one.
Maintained wooden shelves hold tied folios beside their variants. Nothing is written over: additions wait beside the older hands.
A low desk with a sloped folio board and an ink groove. The village scribe makes copies here; the original stays with its bearer.
A broad, scrubbed table for meals shared between shifts in the archive. The folios stay in the reading rooms; ink-stained hands rest here.

Holds three drinks. Fill beside a well, cistern or standing fresh water; a drink relieves one layer of parch.
The edges have browned and curled; the flesh inside is still soft.
A small soot-dark creature with blunt claws and a nose dusted grey from old hearths. It paws through anything left near the cold ash.
A squat earth-grubber with soil worked into the creases of its skin. Its broad claws have loosened more roots than the farmer cares to count.
A narrow line follows the hardened edge. The tang runs through a plain grip to a peened pommel.
A heavy striking head is balanced by a smaller weight below the grip. Both ends are scarred by use.
Closely fitted rings lie in shallow folds. Small overlapping links cover the seams beneath each arm.
Thick overlapping plates are held by broad rivets. Deep straps carry their weight across the shoulders.
Thick glass and a tight stopper. The narrow neck lets you pour without wetting your hands.
Timber rails hang between short posts. A plain latch rests below the top rail.
A fitted panel swings on hinges. A simple latch holds it closed.
A broad marlback with a pale notch cut through one shale back plate. Trained to strike across a two-step gap when armed with a long blade, it watches for a willing ditch mate nearby.
Parallel rake marks cross this short-faced marlback's shoulder plates. It is accustomed to fighting beside a willing companion; separation and cover can break their coordination.
A broken chalk-colored ring follows this viper's low coils. Nearby movement or injury can rouse its ambush; its bite can poison.
A squat four-footed grazer with a blunt muzzle and a ridge of stiff reed-like hair. Its split hooves pick between the worked rows; it shies from close footsteps.
The low reed ridge lies flat against a still, broad body.
A low, narrow hunter with a wedge-shaped muzzle and a tapering tail. Its four feet follow the furrows quietly; a pale jaw opens beneath its dark brow.
A narrow body lies folded over four still feet, its long muzzle resting against the soil.
A shallow stone-lined pocket beside the bank. Its collected water can be drawn into a carried vessel; the wet ground around it is not a refill.
A broad-billed blue-green bird with a pale breast and an uneven fan of tail feathers. It tests loose things with its bill, then tilts its head toward the place where it keeps them.
The broad bill rests against a pale breast. Uneven tail feathers lie spread across the ground.
Ochre burrs hook together above dark, leathery leaves. Gather the hard seeds and brew them alone for a stoneskin tonic; drinking it briefly blunts incoming blows.
Pale crusts collect in the cold shade of stones. Gather the lichen and brew it alone into a freezing coating. Quench a melee weapon with the coating beside a forge; drinking it freezes the drinker.

A narrow-capped marlback with scorched mantle edges and fire-moss tucked into a pouch. It spits a short gob of fire, then closes with its cudgel while its breath returns. Its partner answers nearby attacks; walls interrupt the spit.

A hooded marlback with a stained throat-wrap and a sealed pouch of glimmer brine. It tries to keep three paces while its short acid spray recovers, and steps sideways to clear an ally from its shot. A nearby partner answers attacks, but stone blocks the spray.
A broad hat shades a row of seed pouches. Ask about planting or trade for seeds and a watering grimoire.
A flour-pale cap and a patched apron. Ask about the kitchen, buy a meal, or bring raw food to cook yourself.

Two final remarks occupy opposite pages. A tethered stamp rests beside an unissued cabinet counterfoil. Match each salt-cured subject to the bay bearing their last words, release the haul, then check the filing here. Names are cross-references. Last words are labels, not instructions.
A low chalk-white frame with a slot for a final remark. Haul its corresponding subject onto the marked tile; release the haul before certification.
Four numbered compartments; one counterfoil-shaped lock. Its label reads: MATERIAL ISSUED FOR CORRECTION. Do not return used salt to the unused account.
A stiff card whose punched teeth fit Marrowstye's released-tools cabinet. CERTIFIED POSITION, it says. The wording carefully promises nothing else.
A narrow key with a red cord. The tag warns: DISUSED WING. INCOMPLETE CURE. Unlocking does not make the enclosure safe. Opening releases its occupant.

A pale gate separates the inspection gallery from the empty holding room. Its latch works from either side. Close this gate and the holding room's service gate to enclose an occupant; first get yourself and every loose object clear of the thresholds.

Salt-white bars interrupt the masonry screen along the south passage. This unlocked maintenance entrance bypasses the keyed inspection door. Opening it gives the half-set a path into the service passage. Close it behind you; an occupied threshold cannot be closed.

The wooden gate has dropped off its lower brace. An open gap connects the holding room to the southern service passage. Two sound lengths from the vestibule maintenance rack can brace the frame. Repair permits ordinary opening and closing; it does not close the gate for you or contain anything by itself.

Dry supplies survive behind a buckled salt hood: fire clay, work gloves and an imported sumpsieve dressing. The emergency label says: FOR THE PERSON CONDUCTING THE INSPECTION. The stock is finite; the empty cabinet will remain empty.

Two packets of sootroot pulp and a measure of pitchpod resin sit under a salt-tight lid. These are ink ingredients, reserved for the record that was to follow the inspection. The label reads: COMPLETION MATERIALS. DO NOT USE TO COMPLETE THE SUBJECT. The case stands beyond the central slab; its stock will not be replaced.

Two sound lengths were measured for the holding-room service gate. The sign reads: REPAIR AUTHORISED. ENTRY PENDING REPAIR. This rack is on the safe side of the masonry. The measured lengths match the sagging frame beside the southern passage.

A stone slab has shallow drainage grooves and a single buckle polished brighter than the others. Older holes show where a second set of restraints was removed. A note in Doreth's hand reads: NO SUBJECT RECEIVED BEFORE DEATH. Beneath it, in a different hand: THIS ALSO APPLIES TO REPLACEMENT SUBJECTS. The remaining straps secure vessels during inspection; they cannot restrain a moving creature for you. Deep tendril marks stop against its stone edge. There is room to pass along either side.

A salt-spotted board carries a maintenance sketch, a supply list and an incomplete intake record. A margin sketch records the growth drawing back before it lashes. The board also marks two holding-room gates and the reason the gallery remains closed.

A sieve stands above two shallow trays. Beneath the clean tray: UNUSED. Beneath the other: USED ONCE, STILL DRY. A blunt rake, measuring scoop and tethered stamp have white outlines showing where to return them. These are the staff's working instruments; the bench offers no preservation service.
A short ash handle ends in a broad comb of blunt iron teeth. It levels salt around awkward joints. Heavy enough to use as a cudgel; it cannot preserve a body by itself.

Red cord crosses a barred gate. The plaque reads: INCOMPLETE CURE. MOVEMENT OBSERVED. BLOOM PRESENT. Keep closed. Inspection is optional; opening exposes the public yard. A smaller correction changes SUBJECT RESTLESS to MOTION NOT ATTRIBUTED TO SUBJECT.
Close-set iron rails, heavily salted at the base. The gap is too narrow for a person. A fresh pale cord holds yesterday's inspection card.
A folded receiving copy. Read the salt and carriage accounts; several figures have been carried forward longer than the paper has survived.
Two case numbers have exchanged columns. A careful hand has noted the error without once crossing out a word of the final remarks.
Salt has whitened Doreth's broad apron and settled into the seams of pale gloves. There is a clean patch over each knee. The subjects are handled carefully, whatever the forms call them.
A collar almost reaches Ivrin's ears. Pale gloves hold a ruled board against the chest; its corners have worn the same two places in the coat. The margin contains a very small drawing of a thimble.

Salt covers one shoulder and ends in a damp line across the ribs. Green growth works through the gap; its tendril pulls the human frame after it. An intake tag turns face-in against the chest. This cure was interrupted. The movement is not a response to speech. Before it lashes, a tendril draws straight back. It strikes along that line for two paces, then hangs loose while the tendril gathers again.
Sound lengths sorted out of a fallen frame. Two lengths can brace a jammed wooden gate.
Tough knotflax stems stripped and twisted into cord as they are gathered. One coil can replace a snapped well line.
An ochre bulb under a papery, ribbed skin. Edible raw; roasting beside a cooking fire makes a more nourishing meal.
The split skin holds a soft, sweet center. A small meal that keeps well in its own wrapper.
The pale seam leaks a green sap. Brewers prize its vital character for restorative mixtures.
Paired thick leaves joined by a pale seam. Their vital sap is a brewing ingredient; the raw leaves are not a healing potion.

A lifting frame spans this masonry well. A spindle carries the line and bucket above the water below.
A short timber gate marks the allotment boundary. Cross-braces support its wooden frame around the hinges and latch.
Red clay shows where water has undercut the bank. Gather four measures for repairs; the exposed pocket is finite.
Four sound lengths can be pried from this collapsed frame. Gather them for wooden repairs.

A shallow clay pan for wrapped expedition meals. The open oven beside it remains free to use. Repair the split with two fire clay, then commission Orven: two emberwheat, one claspbean pulp and two drams. A batch takes 120 world ticks. Leave the tied ingredients alone; interruption returns only what remains, and the fee is kept.
The cook ties each paid batch into this tray. Taking or destroying an ingredient cancels that batch; only its surviving ingredients can be recovered.
Finished field meals are left here. Pick up your actual parcel; an empty board cannot make another one. The ordinary trader shelf is separate.

Toasted emberwheat folded around claspbean dressing, tied with a dry leaf. Eat in one action to heal 3d4 and remove one ordinary bleeding effect. It packs smaller than its ingredients; freely toasting the two grains separately yields more healing.

A pigment bowl, resin spoon and tethered bottle clamp. PUBLIC COPIES, the small plaque says. Ivrin combines two sootroot pulp, one pitchpod resin and three drams into one ink vial. The pigment is botanical; no preserved person is an ingredient. Use a vial on a charged book to Re-ink it, or spend it as rental ink.
Two cord loops match the keeper's tied beds. Nella reserves these plants and this tray for gathering partners. Ask her before taking from them. The four open crop beds remain public.

Mud-dark pages show a boot planted at the lip of a ditch and the second foot already across. Read to learn Vault: cross a two-cell distance with a clear landing. The skill does not open doors or promise safety beyond your sight. This practical manual uses no ink charges.

A timber hoist has sagged across the direct approach. Its iron shoe has bitten into the earth. A strong traveler can drag the frame aside; the longer path around its shoulder remains open. The frame itself offers no harvestable reward.

Timber rails span a hinged gap. Sound hinges let the wicket open and close; damaged ones can be braced with two salvaged timber. The longer path around remains open. Breaking the rails leaves a permanent opening.

Thick boards are stacked on two runners, still braced as one heavy pallet. A strong traveler can haul the whole solid load as a movable obstacle. Dismantling it yields exactly two salvaged timber and removes the pallet; the boards cannot be reclaimed twice. Sound timber can restore the buckled garden wicket above.

A taut knotflax loop between low stakes. The first creature crossing it is held in place for two turns, including its maker and allies. A held creature can still attack or cast; the loop does not prolong an existing hold. The cord tears on use and cannot be recovered.
A split glow-quartz shard throws a low, steady light. Its spent glow lasts thirty world turns. It cannot be recovered for another use and does not lure creatures.
